title: Telemetry at two thousand events a second
prompt: Northgate Utilities' 200,000 smart meters send readings every five minutes through Azure IoT Hub (about 2,400 events per second at peak). The platform team wants to filter invalid readings, enrich them with meter metadata, route them into an Eventhouse for operator dashboards, and also land a copy in a lakehouse — all with minimal custom code to maintain. Which engine fits this brief?

options.text: An Eventstream with filter and enrich nodes, routed to Eventhouse and lakehouse destinations.
options.why: Correct. Eventstream is the managed, no-code streaming pipeline for exactly this shape: continuous ingest, light transformation, multi-destination routing.

options.text: A Spark Structured Streaming notebook with custom windowing code.
options.why: Spark streaming suits complex stateful or ML-grade logic; for filter-enrich-route it adds custom code the team does not need.

options.text: A data pipeline with a five-minute scheduled Copy activity.
options.why: A scheduled copy is batch by construction; it neither streams nor keeps the dashboards current between runs.

options.text: A Copy job pointed at IoT Hub.
options.why: Copy jobs move stored data in managed batches; they are not a continuous streaming ingest for telemetry.

explanation: The streaming-engine choice turns on transformation complexity and destination shape: managed light transforms to multiple destinations favors Eventstream; heavy custom stateful logic favors Spark Structured Streaming; anything scheduled is batch, not streaming.

title: Device time or arrival time
prompt: Meters buffer readings during connectivity gaps, so a reading's device timestamp can be up to 45 minutes older than its arrival time. For correct five-minute voltage summaries, which timestamp must the windowing use?

options.text: The device (event) timestamp carried in the payload — windows must bucket events by when they happened, not when they landed.
options.why: Correct. Event time is the only timestamp that reflects the physical interval a reading belongs to; arrival time would mis-bucket every buffered reading.

options.text: The ingestion timestamp, because it is always monotonic.
options.why: Monotonic arrival order says nothing about which measurement interval a reading describes.

options.text: Whichever timestamp is smaller, per event.
options.why: That is event time stated as a heuristic, not a rule, and it breaks when clocks drift the other way.

options.text: The query time, rounding each event to the nearest five-minute boundary at render time.
options.why: Query-time rounding rewrites history on every render and cannot align to the true interval.

explanation: The lesson the RTI Academy keeps repeating: window on event time. With late arrivals, the design question becomes how far back the computation must look — not which clock to trust.

title: Five-minute buckets, no overlap

explanation: Tumbling windows are the fixed, disjoint, clock-aligned bucketing every summary dashboard usually wants; the other three families each answer different questions.

title: The overlap question
prompt: An analyst wants a rolling one-hour voltage average computed every five minutes, so each computation covers the last hour and windows overlap. Which window family fits, and what must the team accept?

options.text: Hopping windows — one-hour size, five-minute hop; each event contributes to several windows.
options.why: Correct. Hopping windows with hop < size overlap by design; every event lands in multiple computations.

options.text: Tumbling windows — five-minute size; the one-hour figure is derived downstream.
options.why: Tumbling buckets do not overlap; deriving an hour from them means aggregating twelve buckets, a different (and legitimate, but different) design.

options.text: Session windows with a one-hour timeout.
options.why: Session windows close on inactivity, not on a schedule; they do not produce a rolling average.

options.text: Tumbling windows with a one-hour size and five-minute alignment.
options.why: That is still one-hour non-overlapping buckets emitted hourly, not a five-minute rolling series.

explanation: Hopping windows are tumbling windows that overlap: size defines the coverage, hop the emission cadence, and events legitimately count in multiple windows.

title: Counting the overlap honestly
prompt: A hopping window (size 1 hour, hop 5 minutes) counts anomaly events. An anomalous reading arrives at 10:03. In how many window results does it participate, and what does the team need to remember when reading totals?

options.text: Up to 12 windows cover it (one per hop within the hour); raw window counts must not be summed as unique events.
options.why: Correct. With size 60 and hop 5, an event lies inside up to size/hop windows — summing window outputs double-counts by design.

options.text: Exactly one — hopping windows assign each event to its nearest hop.
options.why: That is tumbling behavior; hopping deliberately overlaps.

options.text: Zero, because the event arrived between hops.
options.why: Windows are computed over covered intervals; arrival between hops does not exclude the event.

options.text: Exactly two — the window it opens and the window it closes.
options.why: The overlap span is size/hop, not two.

explanation: Hopping-window overlap is arithmetic: an event participates in up to size/hop windows. Aggregate outputs are per-window views, never additive across windows.

title: Tumbling buckets in KQL
prompt: Which KQL fragment produces per-five-minute average voltage over the last hour from meter_readings?

options.text: meter_readings | where Timestamp > ago(1h) | summarize avg(Voltage) by bin(Timestamp, 5m)
options.why: Correct. bin() buckets the event-time column into aligned five-minute intervals and summarize aggregates per bucket.

options.text: meter_readings | summarize avg(Voltage) by Timestamp
options.why: Grouping by the raw timestamp yields one bucket per distinct event time — no windowing at all.

options.text: meter_readings | where Timestamp > ago(1h) | count
options.why: That returns a single row with the total count; no time axis survives.

options.text: meter_readings | project Timestamp, Voltage | take 100
options.why: project/take shape a row sample; nothing is aggregated.

explanation: The KQL idiom for tumbling windows is summarize over bin(timestamp, size): aligned buckets with an aggregate each — the pattern the RTI tutorial builds dashboards on.

meter_readings
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
